terms.grammar: adjective; the person to whom it is known in the dative
evidence: Cic. Mil. 76: quae nōta sunt omnibus (Lewis & Short, s.v. nōscō)
Cic. Sull. 72: vīta P. Sullae vōbīs populōque Rōmānō nōtissima
terms.comment: The plain word: mihi nōtus est, “I know him, he’s familiar to me”. Ignōtus is unfamiliar.

evidence: Petr. 100: vōx auribus meīs familiāris (Lewis & Short)
Quint. 5.10.96: familiāribus magis eī aetātī exemplīs
terms.comment: First “of the household” (rēs familiāris, one’s property), then “intimate, friendly”, and as a noun a close friend (Cic. Lael. 39). The sense “well known, familiar” to the ears or the mind is post-Augustan (Petronius, Quintilian); in Cicero’s Latin say nōtus.

phrases.latin: fingī haec putātis, quae patent, quae nōta sunt omnibus, quae tenentur?
phrases.english: do you think these things are invented, which are plain, which everyone knows, which are proved?

sources: Lewis & Short: nosco · Lewis & Short: familiaris
Cicero, Petronius and Quintilian quoted as Lewis & Short quotes them.
The example sentence marked “composed” is ours.
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 337.
